messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 59
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Professor
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 54

He is a 59-year-old African man who has built much of his identity around steadiness, thoughtfulness, and control. As a professor, he is used to speaking carefully, organizing ideas, and guiding others through difficult material. For years he moves through his work with a quiet authority, arriving prepared, answering questions with patience, and keeping his private life largely separate from the classroom. He lives alone and has long accepted his single life as manageable, even purposeful. That sense of order is shaken by what happens to someone he loves deeply.

The traumatic event is not something that happens directly to him, but it changes his world in the same immediate way. A loved one is harmed, and he learns of it with the kind of shock that makes time feel unreal. In the hours and days afterward, he keeps returning to the same moment of hearing the news, as if his mind is trying to locate the point where things went wrong. He recalls the room, the sound of the voice telling him, the way his body seemed to go numb before the meaning fully arrived. He describes feeling split in two: one part of him moving through the practical steps that needed to be taken, another part standing helplessly outside the scene, unable to accept that it is happening.

In the beginning he functions because he has to. He makes calls, answers questions, and attends to details with the disciplined precision that others expect from him. Colleagues notice that he is present but distant, courteous but withdrawn. He continues lecturing, yet the classroom no longer feels familiar. At times he catches himself staring at notes without absorbing them, losing his place in a sentence, then recovering with a slight laugh that masks his embarrassment. He becomes more guarded with students and stops lingering after class. The work that once gave him structure now requires an effort that leaves him exhausted by the end of the day.

At home, the silence is harder. He finds himself checking his phone repeatedly, sometimes without realizing he is doing it. He rereads messages, listens carefully to voicemails, and becomes tense when the telephone rings unexpectedly. He avoids places and conversations that bring the loved one sharply to mind, but avoidance gives him little relief. Instead, the memories come on their own, often in fragments: a hospital corridor, a particular smell, the expression on another person’s face. When they arrive, he feels his chest tighten and his thoughts race toward the same helpless question of what else he should have done. He does not describe himself as emotional, yet he notices that he is more easily stirred to tears when alone, especially at night.

Sleep becomes difficult. He falls asleep late and wakes early, sometimes with vivid dreams that leave him disoriented and sweating. On waking, he must orient himself to the room and remember where he is before he can get out of bed. During the day he is jumpy in a way that surprises him; sudden noises make him tense, and he finds himself scanning rooms instinctively, as though danger might appear without warning. His body feels persistently on alert. He walks more slowly through crowds, chooses seats with his back to the wall, and becomes impatient with any unexpected change in plans.

He also becomes more irritable with people close to him, though he dislikes this change in himself. Small frustrations feel larger than before. He may snap at a colleague over an ordinary scheduling issue, then spend hours replaying the interaction and feeling ashamed. His self-criticism is severe. He tells himself that as an educated man he should be able to handle grief more gracefully, but this only deepens his sense of failure. Beneath that criticism is a heavier feeling that he has not been able to protect someone important to him, and that helplessness remains close to the surface.

Over time, the life he had before the trauma begins to feel distant, almost belonging to another person. He still teaches, still manages his responsibilities, but with a narrowed range of energy. Joy feels muted. He can remember what it was like to feel open and engaged, yet now he moves through days with vigilance and a persistent ache that he does not easily name. Even in conversation, he seems to be listening from somewhere slightly removed, as if part of him is always waiting for the next blow.
